{{Short description|Extension of independent vectors to bases}}
The '''Steinitz exchange lemma''' is a theorem in [[linear algebra]] concerning [[Basis (linear algebra)|bases]], [[Dimension (vector space)|dimensionality]] of a [[vector space]], stating that for any set smaller than a spanning set, there is a set of vectors in the spanning set but missing from the smaller set that can be added to the smaller set to make that set spanning as well. 

It can be used, for example, to show that any two bases for a finite-dimensional vector space have the same number of elements. The result is named after the German mathematician [[Ernst Steinitz]]. The result is often called the '''Steinitz–Mac&nbsp;Lane exchange lemma''', also recognizing the generalization<ref>
{{citation|last=Mac&nbsp;Lane|first=Saunders|authorlink=Saunders Mac Lane|year=1936|title=Some interpretations of abstract linear dependence in terms of projective geometry|journal=American Journal of Mathematics|volume=58|pages=236–240|doi=10.2307/2371070| jstor=2371070 | issue=1|publisher=The Johns Hopkins University Press}}.</ref>
by [[Saunders Mac Lane]]
of Steinitz's lemma to [[matroid]]s.<ref>
{{citation|editor-last=Kung|editor-first=Joseph P. S.|title=A Source Book in Matroid Theory|publisher=Birkhäuser|mr=0890330|isbn=0-8176-3173-9|location=Boston|year=1986|doi=10.1007/978-1-4684-9199-9|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/sourcebookinmatr0000kung|doi-access=free}}.
</ref>

== Statement ==
Let <math>U</math> and <math>W</math> be finite subsets of a vector space <math>V</math>. If <math>U</math> is a set of [[Linear independence|linearly independent]] vectors, and <math>W</math> [[Linear span|spans]] <math>V</math>, then:

1. <math>|U| \leq |W|</math>;

2. There is a set <math>W' \subseteq W</math> with <math>|W'|=|W|-|U|</math> such that <math>U \cup W'</math> spans <math>V</math>.

==Proof==

Suppose <math>U=\{u_1, \dots, u_m\}</math> and <math>W=\{w_1, \dots, w_n\}</math>. We wish to show that <math>m \le n</math>, and that after rearranging the <math>w_j</math> if necessary, the set <math>\{u_1, \dotsc, u_m, w_{m + 1}, \dotsc, w_n\}</math> spans <math>V</math>. We proceed by [[mathematical induction|induction]] on <math>m</math>.

For the base case, suppose <math>m</math> is zero.
In this case, the claim holds because there are no vectors <math>u_i</math>, and the set <math>\{w_1, \dotsc, w_n\}</math> spans <math>V</math> by hypothesis.

For the inductive step, assume the proposition is true for <math>m-1</math>. By the inductive hypothesis we may reorder the <math>w_i</math> so that <math>\{ u_1,\ldots, u_{m-1},w_{m},\ldots,w_n\}</math> spans <math>V</math>. Since <math>u_{m}\in V</math>, there exist coefficients <math>\mu_1, \ldots, \mu_n </math> such that
:<math>u_{m}=\sum_{i=1}^{m-1} \mu_i u_i+\sum_{j=m}^n \mu_j w_j</math>.
At least one of the <math>\mu_j </math> for <math>j \ge m</math> must be non-zero, since otherwise this equality would contradict the linear independence of <math>\{ u_1,\ldots,u_{m} \}</math>; this also shows that indeed <math>m \le n.</math> By reordering <math>\mu_{m}w_{m},\ldots,\mu_{n}w_n</math> if necessary, we may assume that <math>\mu_{m}</math> is nonzero. Therefore, we have
: <math>w_{m}= \frac{1}{\mu_{m}}\left(u_{m} - \sum_{j=1}^{m-1} \mu_j u_j - \sum_{j=m+1}^n \mu_j w_j\right)</math>.
In other words, <math>w_{m}</math> is in the span of <math>\{ u_1,\ldots, u_{m},w_{m+1},\ldots,w_n\}</math>. Since this span contains each of the vectors <math> u_1, \ldots, u_{m-1}, w_{m}, w_{m+1}, \ldots, w_n </math>, by the inductive hypothesis it contains <math>V</math>.

==Applications==
The Steinitz exchange lemma is a basic result in [[computational mathematics]], especially in [[numerical linear algebra|linear algebra]] and in [[Matroid#Greedy_algorithm|combinatorial algorithms]].<ref>Page v in Stiefel:
{{cite book|last=Stiefel|first=Eduard L.|authorlink=Eduard Stiefel|title=An introduction to numerical mathematics|url=https://archive.org/details/introductiontonu1963stie|url-access=registration|edition=Translated by Werner C. Rheinboldt & Cornelie J. Rheinboldt from the second German|publisher=Academic Press|location=New York|year=1963|pages=x+286|mr=181077}}
</ref>
